        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script). It covers everything you asked for: | Step | What to do | Command / File | |------|------------|----------------| | 1 | **Clone the repo** | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` | | 2 | **Analyse & create artefacts** | – Dockerfile
– Kubernetes YAMLs
– GitHub Actions workflow | | 3 | **Stage the new files** | `git add Dockerfile k8s/ deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml` | | 4 | **Commit & push** | `git commit -m "Add Docker, K8s, CI"`
`git push origin main` | --- ## 1. Clone the repository ```bash git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git cd nodejs-welcome ``` > **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use HTTPS instead: > `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` --- ## 2. Analyse the repo & create artefacts ### 2.1 Dockerfile The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`) with a `package.json`. A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile for Node.js looks like this: ```dockerfile # Dockerfile # ------------------------------------ # 1️⃣ Use an official Node runtime as a parent image FROM node:18-alpine AS builder # 2️⃣ Set working directory WORKDIR /usr/src/app # 3️⃣ Install app dependencies COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --only=production # 4️⃣ Copy app source COPY . . # 5️⃣ Expose the port the app listens on EXPOSE 3000 # 6️⃣ Start the app CMD ["node", "app.js"] ``` > **Why `node:18-alpine`?** > Alpine images are small, secure, and the latest LTS (18.x) is stable for most Node apps. > **If you want a multi‑stage build** (to keep the final image tiny) you can add a second stage that copies only the built artefacts. For this simple app the single‑stage approach above is fine. ### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs Create a directory `k8s/` and add `deployment.yaml`: ```yaml # k8s/deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nodejs-welcome labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: nodejs-welcome template: metadata: labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: containers: - name: nodejs-welcome image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest # <-- replace with your registry ports: - containerPort: 3000 env: - name: NODE_ENV value: production --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nodejs-welcome spec: type: ClusterIP selector: app: nodejs-welcome ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 3000 ``` > **What this does** > * Deployment: 2 replicas of the container, each listening on port 3000. > * Service: Exposes the pods on port 80 inside the cluster (ClusterIP). > * Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image you’ll push. ### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: ```yaml # .github/workflows/ci.yml name: Build & Push Docker Image on: push: branches: - main jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: # Checkout the repo - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 # Log in to GitHub Container Registry - name: Log in to GHCR uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} # Build the Docker image - name: Build Docker image run: | docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest . # Push the image - name: Push Docker image run: | docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest ``` > **How it works** > * Triggered on pushes to `main`. > * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR. > * Builds the image from the Dockerfile in the repo root. > * Pushes the image to `ghcr.io//:latest`. > **If you prefer Docker Hub** replace the login and image names accordingly. --- ## 3. Stage the new files ```bash git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml ``` --- ## 4. Commit & push ```bash git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow" git push origin main ``` > After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to GHCR. --- ### Quick sanity check ```bash # Verify Dockerfile builds locally docker build -t nodejs-welcome-test . # Run the container locally docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome-test ``` Open `http://localhost:3000` – you should see the app’s response. --- ### Done! You now have: * A production‑ready Dockerfile * Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs * A CI workflow that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` * All changes committed and pushed to the repo Happy coding!
